shared_framework.heading: The India entry framework - six phases, every one ends in a named deliverable
shared_framework.note: Render on all three landing pages as numbered steps, preceded by the page's method_intro line.

phases.title: Business assessment
phases.text: Working sessions inside your business: portfolio, pricing, capacity, export experience and India ambitions - so the entry plan fits the company you actually are. Deliverable: assessment memo and scope lock.

phases.title: Opportunity sizing and validation
phases.text: Category demand, price-tier fit and channel potential validated through primary research in India - buyer, retailer and distributor interviews, not database downloads. Deliverable: opportunity report with a Go / No-Go recommendation.

phases.title: Competitive and regulatory intelligence
phases.text: Competitor route-to-market mapping, trade margin benchmarks, and the regulatory pathway - certification applicability, import duty structure, labelling - resolved before commitments. Deliverable: competitive map and regulatory register.

phases.title: GTM and commercial design
phases.text: Price-pack architecture for Indian tiers, channel sequencing, revenue projection framework and working capital visibility. Deliverable: entry roadmap with commercial model.

phases.title: Distributor search and appointment
phases.text: 200-300 candidates longlisted from field networks, scored to a 20-30 shortlist on capability, then negotiated - performance gates, data rights, exit mechanics - to 2-3 signed partnerships. Deliverable: signed distribution agreements.

phases.title: Launch and governance
phases.text: Launch calendar, sales cadence, partner scorecards and review governance for the first 90 days - expansion gated on milestones. Deliverable: operating launch plan and governance system.

tiers.name: Diagnostic
tiers.text: Opportunity sizing and market validation only - the lowest-commitment way to get an evidence-based Go / No-Go before bigger decisions.

tiers.name: Full market entry
tiers.text: Assessment through signed distributor appointments - the complete six-phase engagement, fixed-fee by phase.

tiers.name: Post-launch retainer

faq.q: How do Japanese companies typically enter the Indian market?
faq.a: Most successful entries in distributor-led categories follow the same path: opportunity validation, regulatory clearance run in parallel, then a scored distributor search to signed appointment - with a subsidiary considered only after channel proof. Direct subsidiary-first entries suit companies with existing India revenue or service obligations; our route-options framework prices both against your case.

faq.q: How do we find a trustworthy distributor in India from Japan?
faq.a: Not from exhibition booths: field-network longlisting of 200-300 candidates, capability scoring to 20-30, reference checks with current principals and retailers, then negotiation with performance gates and exit mechanics. Trust is engineered through process, and the scoring is shared with you at every stage.

faq.q: Does BIS certification apply to our products?
faq.a: It depends on category - BIS mandatory certification lists cover electronics, toys, steel products, appliances and more, and Chinese-origin components in Japanese-assembled products raise additional scrutiny. We resolve applicability in phase 3 and coordinate certified filing partners where needed, before any inventory moves.

faq.q: How long does India market entry take for a Japanese company?
faq.a: Diagnostic: 3-4 weeks. Full entry through signed distributor appointments: typically 4-6 months depending on category and certification lead times. First revenue timing then depends on channel type - our roadmaps set it against milestones, not hope.

faq.q: Do you work with JETRO and Japanese trade bodies?

Trade bodies open doors and provide market perspective; our role is the on-the-ground work those introductions need next: validation, distributor search and appointment.

faq.q: How do I find a distributor in India for my product?
faq.a: Field-network longlisting (not directory scrapes), capability audit across infrastructure, category depth, financial capacity and reference checks made with retailers and current principals, then benchmarked negotiation. The process runs 8-14 weeks; shortcuts show up as disputes in year two.

faq.q: What does a distributor search service cost in India?
faq.a: We work fixed-fee by engagement scope - shared in the first call - and take no placement or success fees from distributors, so the recommendation is never for sale. Against the cost of one failed appointment (typically 18-24 lost months plus brand damage), the fee is the cheap part of the decision.

faq.q: What commission or margin do Indian distributors take?
faq.a: General trade FMCG typically runs 5-8% distributor and 10-15% retailer margins; equipment and specialty categories run wider distributor margins against service obligations; modern trade and e-commerce add promotion loads. We build your full channel waterfall from live trade interviews before pricing is locked - and benchmark every term against our mandate data.

faq.q: Should we appoint one national distributor or several regional ones?
faq.a: Rarely one, at entry: performance-gated regional appointments preserve leverage and let evidence allocate territory. National exclusivity is something a partner earns with velocity, not a signing incentive - and the agreement should say so explicitly.

faq.q: Can you manage the distributor relationship after signing?

pages.h1: How to enter the Indian market - four routes, one honest comparison
pages.sub: Most India entry advice sells you the route the adviser happens to sell. We execute all four - distributor-led, wholly-owned subsidiary, joint venture and digital-first - so the comparison on this page is a framework, not a funnel. Bring your numbers; the right route falls out.

who_this_is_for.title: First-time India entrants
who_this_is_for.text: The route decision shapes everything downstream - tax, control, speed, working capital. It deserves a framework before it gets an opinion.

why_now.heading: The four routes - what each buys and costs
points: Distributor-led: fastest to revenue, lowest fixed cost, least control - right for brand and product companies in channel-led categories testing depth before committing capital.

Wholly-owned subsidiary: full control and margin, 3-6 months to operational, carries compliance overhead and working capital - right when service obligations, enterprise sales or manufacturing demand presence.

Joint venture: solves real constraints (regulated sectors, government proximity, manufacturing scale) at the price of governance complexity - right when the partner brings something you verifiably cannot build.
Digital-first: marketplaces and D2C validate demand at the lowest entry cost in eligible categories - right as a proving ground, rarely as the end state.

pages.method_intro: Phases 1-4 of our framework drive this decision: your business reality, validated demand, the regulatory map and the commercial model - then the route is arithmetic, not argument.

regulatory.heading: The structures behind the routes
regulatory.text: FDI entry rules (automatic route for most sectors, approval route for a defined list), subsidiary formation and compliance obligations, JV governance and exit design, import structures for distributor-led models, and marketplace eligibility rules for digital-first entries - mapped in phase 3 so the route decision is made with the legal reality priced in. We coordinate specialist legal and tax partners for formal structuring.

Metro-first, capability-led distribution reaching first revenue inside 120 days without an entity commitment.

pages.transparency: The route decision is the core of our Diagnostic tier: 3-4 weeks, fixed fee, ending in a route recommendation with your numbers in the model and an implementation plan for the chosen path. If the answer is 'not yet', we say so - a funded defer with a trigger beats a proud entry into the wrong year.

faq.q: What is the best way to enter the Indian market?
faq.a: The one your category, capital and control needs select - distributor-led for channel categories testing depth, subsidiary for service-heavy and enterprise models, JV where regulation or scale demands a partner, digital-first as a low-cost proving ground. Generic answers are how wrong routes get chosen; the framework on this page exists to replace them.

faq.q: Can a foreign company sell in India without a local entity?
faq.a: Yes - through distributors and importers-of-record in most categories, and through marketplace structures in eligible ones. Entity formation becomes necessary when service obligations, enterprise contracts or manufacturing enter the picture; sequencing it after channel proof is often the capital-efficient path.

faq.q: How much FDI is allowed in India and through which route?
faq.a: Most sectors permit 100% FDI through the automatic route; a defined list (defence beyond thresholds, insurance, multi-brand retail among them) requires government approval or carries caps. The practical question is rarely the ceiling - it is the structure and compliance design underneath it, which we map before the route decision.

faq.q: When should we switch from a distributor to our own subsidiary?
faq.a: When the arithmetic flips: channel margin retained exceeds subsidiary running costs at your volume, or when service, enterprise or product-line decisions demand control. We model the crossover point explicitly - switching too early burns capital, too late burns growth.

faq.q: Is a joint venture necessary to do business in India?
faq.a: In most sectors, no - the mandatory-JV era ended years ago. A JV is justified only when the partner solves a verifiable constraint: regulatory access, manufacturing scale, government proximity. 'It felt safer' is the most expensive JV rationale in India's corporate history.

pages.meta_title: BIS Certification for Foreign Products Entering India - The Basics | GreyRadius
pages.meta_description: Does BIS certification apply to your product? Mandatory certification lists, the foreign manufacturer pathway, Chinese-origin component questions, timelines and costs - explained for exporters entering India.
pages.h1: BIS certification for foreign products entering India - what exporters need to know

sections.h2: What BIS certification is and when it is mandatory
sections.body: The Bureau of Indian Standards operates mandatory certification schemes covering an expanding list of product categories - electronics and IT hardware, toys, steel products, appliances, footwear, chemicals and more. If your product appears in a mandatory list (under the ISI mark scheme or the Compulsory Registration Scheme for electronics), it cannot legally be imported or sold in India without certification. The lists expand through Quality Control Orders issued sector by sector, which means a product exempt last year may be covered this year - applicability must be checked against current orders, not past experience.

Foreign manufacturers certify through the Foreign Manufacturers Certification Scheme: application, factory audit by BIS officials at your overseas plant, product testing in BIS-recognised labs, and an Indian authorised representative to hold local responsibility. Plan realistically for a multi-month process - audit scheduling for overseas plants is the common bottleneck - and treat the authorised representative decision seriously: that entity carries compliance obligations on your behalf.

A recurring issue for Japanese, Korean and Southeast Asian exporters: products assembled at home with Chinese-origin components face additional scrutiny at Indian customs, and in some categories the component origin affects certification and import treatment. This is answerable - with component-level documentation, origin mapping and correct declarations prepared in advance. Discovered at port, the same question strands inventory; resolved in planning, it is paperwork.

sections.h2: Timelines, costs and the sequencing mistake
sections.body: Certification timelines run from weeks (registration schemes with existing test reports) to several months (factory-audit routes for first-time applicants). The sequencing mistake we see repeatedly: companies sign distributors, book launch dates and then start certification - putting a regulator on the critical path of a commercial promise. The correct order runs certification applicability in the same phase as market validation, files early for covered products, and lets the launch calendar absorb reality instead of colliding with it.

sections.h2: How this fits an entry plan
sections.body: In our India entry framework, regulatory intelligence is phase 3 - run in parallel with commercial design, so distributor negotiations and certification progress together. Where formal filings are needed we coordinate specialist certification partners while owning the overall pathway. If you are assessing whether BIS applies to your product line, that answer is part of our 3-4 week Diagnostic - along with whether the market case justifies the filing at all.

pages.cta_line: Assessing India entry for a certification-covered product? The Diagnostic answers applicability and opportunity together.

faq.q: How long does BIS certification take for a foreign company?
faq.a: From a few weeks under registration schemes (electronics with ready test reports) to several months under factory-audit routes - overseas audit scheduling is the usual bottleneck. File early and keep certification off your launch-critical path.

faq.q: Do products with Chinese components need special treatment at Indian customs?
faq.a: They face additional scrutiny in several categories, and origin can affect certification and duty treatment. Component-level origin documentation prepared in advance turns a port problem into paperwork.

pages.meta_title: Distributor Margins in India - Economics and Benchmarks for Foreign Brands | GreyRadius
pages.meta_description: What Indian distributors actually earn and expect - margin benchmarks by channel, credit cycle realities, trade spend loads and the agreement terms that matter more than margin. From live mandate data.
pages.h1: Distributor economics in India - the benchmarks foreign brands negotiate blind

sections.h2: The margin waterfall nobody shows you
sections.body: Foreign brands negotiate Indian distribution agreements knowing their home-market margins and almost nothing else. The Indian waterfall differs by channel: general trade FMCG typically runs 5-8% distributor margin and 10-15% retailer margin; specialty and equipment categories run wider distributor margins (often 15-30%) against service and inventory obligations; modern trade adds listing fees and promotion participation; quick commerce and e-commerce load commissions and advertising on top. The number that matters is not any single margin - it is your landed-cost-to-consumer-price waterfall, built line by line for each channel you intend to use.

sections.h2: Credit cycles - the term that sinks entrants
sections.body: Indian trade runs on credit: distributor-to-retailer credit of 15-45 days is standard, and distributors pass working capital pressure upstream. Foreign brands accustomed to letter-of-credit exports discover that competitive Indian terms mean funding the channel - and the entrants who ignore this choke at month six, precisely when velocity starts. Working capital design belongs in the entry model, not in the first crisis call.

sections.h2: Trade spend is a load, not an option
sections.body: Schemes, retailer margins on promotions, visibility payments and launch support are structural in Indian trade - budget them as a percentage of revenue from day one. Brands that arrive with ex-factory pricing logic and no trade-spend line either lose shelf presence or destroy their own margin reacting quarter by quarter.

sections.h2: The five clauses worth more than two margin points
sections.body: Across our mandates, the agreements that age well share five clauses: performance gates with defined consequences, customer and sell-through data rights, pricing control boundaries, explicit marketing obligations, and exit mechanics including stock buy-back terms. Margin is the loud negotiation; these five are the quiet ones that decide who owns your market when the honeymoon ends. Distributors negotiate these agreements every month; foreign brands negotiate them once - benchmarks are how the asymmetry gets corrected.

sections.h2: Using benchmarks in a live negotiation
sections.body: We maintain distributor economics benchmarks from live mandates - margins by channel and category, credit norms, trade spend loads, gate structures - and carry them into every negotiation we run. The predictable result: terms typically improve by more than the cost of the engagement, and both sides sign an agreement that survives, because it was priced on evidence rather than bravado. The full benchmark sheet is part of our distribution partner development engagements; the Diagnostic includes a category-specific view.

pages.cta_line: Negotiating Indian distribution terms this quarter? Ask for the category benchmark view before you table numbers.

faq.q: What margin should I offer an Indian distributor?
faq.a: Channel and category set the band: 5-8% in general trade FMCG, 15-30% in specialty and equipment against service obligations - but the right answer comes from your full waterfall and what you are asking the partner to fund and do. Benchmarks beat guesses; obligations should price into margin explicitly.

faq.q: What payment terms do Indian distributors expect from foreign brands?
faq.a: Advance or LC terms are achievable at entry but cost you partner quality and velocity; competitive terms mean extending credit as trust builds, typically staged against performance. Design the credit path into the agreement rather than discovering it in renegotiation.
